title: A puzzle about seven bridges in one city gave birth to graph theory
body: Königsberg, now Kaliningrad in Russia, straddled the Pregel River, with two islands, Kneiphof and Lomse, joined to each other and to the banks by seven bridges. Could a walk cross each bridge exactly once? In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved it impossible: passing through a landmass uses two bridges, in and out, so any landmass with an **odd number of bridges** must be where the walk starts or ends. A walk has at most two ends, yet all four landmasses were odd: five bridges on one, three on each of the others. It counts as the first theorem of graph theory.

slides.alt: Schematic map of Königsberg: a river with north and south banks and two islands, Kneiphof and Lomse, connected by seven bridges. Each landmass is labelled with its bridge count: Kneiphof 5, Lomse 3, north bank 3, south bank 3.
slides.caption: Four landmasses, each with an odd number of bridges.

slides.heading: Euler’s argument
items: Passing through a landmass uses two bridges: one in, one out
So a landmass with an odd number of bridges must be a start or an end
A walk has at most two ends
All four landmasses were odd (5, 3, 3, 3), so no such walk exists

slides.heading: The bridges today
slides.text: Two of the seven bridges did not survive the bombing of the city in the Second World War, and two more were later demolished for a highway. With the bridges that stand today, a walk crossing each once is possible, but it has to begin on one island and end on the other.

slides.question: How many bridges touched the island of Kneiphof?
slides.explanation: Kneiphof had five bridges: two to each bank and one to Lomse. The other three landmasses had three each, so every count was odd.
